raw_response:
I'm 73 this year, and I've been farming these 4 mu of land for half a century. My wife and I are the only ones left at home now — our children work in the city and send a little money, but not much. I went to school for a few years when I was young, just enough to read a newspaper and do simple sums. I don't trust all these new ideas; I trust what I've seen with my own eyes on this field.

For the winter wheat, I'll plant around October 8th, same as always. I save my own wheat seed — why spend money buying new when my seed grows fine? Before planting, I'll spread about half a bag of compound fertilizer per mu (that's the 100-jin bag, so about 50 jin per mu) and plow it in with the small tractor. At greening time in March, if the wheat looks yellow, I'll topdress with urea — maybe 30 jin per mu. If it rains well I might skip it, but usually I do it to be safe. Another 20 jin at jointing if the plants look strong. I irrigate three times: once before winter to protect the seedlings, once at greening, and once at jointing. Water costs more now with the meters, but I can't risk drought. For harvest in early June, I'll probably hire the combine — at my age I can't swing a scythe like I used to, and my wife's back isn't good either.

The maize is harder because the window is so tight. As soon as the wheat comes off in June, I need to get the maize in the ground within three or four days. I hire the tractor man to do a quick rotary till, then I plant hybrid maize seed — I buy this, about 3 jin per mu, costs around 50 yuan per mu. I put down compound fertilizer at planting, about 40 jin per mu, and then topdress with urea at the big flare stage, maybe 25 jin per mu. I irrigate twice if it doesn't rain in July. I spray herbicide once, and if I see armyworms I'll spray insecticide too. 

Money is my biggest worry. My pension is only 150 yuan a month. I can't afford to waste anything. I'd rather put a bit more fertilizer than risk a bad yield — a hungry year hurts more than saving a few yuan. But I also can't spend like the young business farmers with their big machines. I do what I can with my own two hands and what little cash I have.
